newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian opposition leaders hide after police threat.
newsitem.headline: Zambian opposition leaders hide after police threat.

text.p: Three leaders of one of Zambia's main opposition parties went into hiding on Monday after police raided the offices of two election watchdog groups following last week's polls disputed by some groups.

The Zambian government also froze the bank accounts of the Afronet human rights group, which joined opposition parties in their refusal to endorse the landslide re-election of President Frederick Chiluba in polls the opposition said were flawed.
Chiluba's only serious opponent, Kenneth Kaunda, was barred from standing by a new law.

Zambia Democratic Congress president Dean Mungomba and two other leading officals Azwell Banda and Andrew Banda, who warned their party would resort to violence unless the government called fresh elections, went into hiding when they heard police had prepared dockets charging them with treason.

"The three officials went underground after police made several attempts to arrest them from their homes over the weekend. They do not want to be detained without trial for a long time as has been the practice over the past few years," party scretary-general Derrick Chitala told Reuters.
He said the treason charges arose from statements they made last week accusing Chiluba's ruling Movement for Multi-Party Democracy (MMD) of rigging the elections.

Witnesses said earlier on Monday that police seized documents from the offices of the umbrella Committee for a Clean Campaign (CCC) before searching the offices of the Zambia Independent Monitoring Team.
The raids followed the release on Sunday night of the groups' leaders, arrested earlier in the day.
Ngande Mwanajiti, of the CCC group of 19 non-governmental and civic groups that monitored the ballot, and ZIMT's Alfred Zulu were picked up by police for questioning on Sunday morning.
Lawyers present during the search of the CCC offices accused Chiluba's government of trying to silence criticism of the elections, marred by poor turnout and an opposition boycott.
"The searches are nothing but legalised break-ins," CCC lawyer Sakwiba Sikota said.
His group was one of several that accused the government of abusing state resources and using state media to tilt in the favour of the MMD.
Local and foreign election observers said the actual voting last Monday was mostly in order.

"Father of the Nation" Kaunda was excluded by law from standing for the presidency and most opposition parties called on supporters to stay away in protest. They have also threatened to continue a campaign of civil disobedience.
Police gave no comment on the detentions or searches.

Half of Zambia's 4.6 million eligible voters were excluded from the rolls because of flawed registration, but Chiluba rejected opposition criticism and took his oath of office for a second term on Thursday.
He has placed security forces on alert for political unrest.
